findings.where: Step 3 'Mean of a sine wave' text ('A heater warms both ways, so for its size take the mean over half a cycle') and explain paragraph 3 ('Yet the current warms a heater both ways, so for its size the mean is taken over half a cycle')
findings.what: This makes heating the reason for the half-cycle mean, but step 5 then says heating goes with the current squared and needs the RMS, so Dan meets two answers to 'which number tells the heating'; give the half-cycle mean its own reason (a whole-cycle mean of 0 says nothing about how big the current is, so take the half where it flows one way) and keep the heater for the RMS.

findings.where: Step 9 'Form factor' text ('Textbooks call RMS ÷ mean the form factor'), explain paragraph 4 ('textbooks add that the RMS value ÷ the mean value is called the form factor') and the step 10 puzzle 'Its form factor'
findings.what: The definition form factor = RMS ÷ mean has no footnote, because the research notes hold only the MCA line naming the term (source 9), yet step 10's answer rests on that definition alone and Dan's exam asks him to calculate it; cite a source that defines it, or label it unsourced and do not make it the only support for a puzzle answer.

findings.where: Step 3 text and explain paragraph 3 ('Textbooks add that a generator's a.c. is close to a sine wave')
findings.what: This follows ARCHITECTURE's 'textbooks add' rule, but the i8 and i9 reviews asked for such lines to be cited where a source exists, so cite one for it if research finds one.

findings.where: Step 5 'Square, mean, root' text ('Any ramp gives its peak ÷ √3')
findings.what: The screen states the general ramp rule but works only the 6 A ramp, and step 12's sawtooth puzzle depends on the rule; the working (i = A × t ÷ T, mean square A² ÷ 3) is only in the explain, so add it as one working row on the screen.

The screen goes from 'heat goes with the current squared' straight to 'square, find its mean, take the root', leaving out the step the explain gives (a steady I gives I²R, so it heats the same when I² equals the mean of i²); add that clause.

findings.where: Step 1 'The mean value' text ('moves 2³ = 8 C of charge')
findings.what: The reverse rule step (3t² becomes t³) is not shown, though step 2 shows the same move ('turns t² into t³ ÷ 3'), so add it to make 2³ traceable.

findings.where: Step 7 'The fold' text ('Why it fits: a sine wave is the height of a point going steadily round a circle of radius 10 ...')
findings.what: The Pythagoras reason depends on a circle that is never drawn, for a learner who has not done trigonometry; draw a small circle with the point, its height and its sideways distance beside the wave, or introduce it as 'One way to picture why', as the explain does (the maths checks out: sin² + cos² gives square now + square a quarter cycle on = 100).

findings.where: Step 9 'Form factor', the three small graphs
findings.what: Each graph is 110 units high for 20 A, so the ramp's mean (3 A) and RMS (3.46 A) lines are about 2.5 px apart, the sine's (6.37 A and 7.07 A) about 4 px apart, and on the square wave the mean, the RMS and the wave all lie at 10 A; the picture cannot show the gap the form factor measures, and only the table under it shows it, so make the graphs taller or draw only the positive half.
In a lesson that keeps saying 'its square' and 'the squared wave', a column headed 'Square' can be read as a squared current, so head it 'Square wave'.

findings.where: Step 9 'Form factor' text ('The square wave is always 10 A one way or the other, so squaring changes nothing')
findings.what: Squaring does change −10 to 100, so say its size is always 10 A, which makes its half-cycle mean and its RMS both 10 A.

findings.where: Step 9 'Form factor', the time labels under the small graphs
findings.what: The square wave's '1 cycle' (right-aligned at 162) and the sine's '0' (left-aligned at 172) are 10 units apart, so at 360 px they can read as one label, '1 cycle 0'; drop the inner '0's or widen the gaps.

findings.where: Step 12 'A sawtooth', the working row 'A ramp from 0 V to 30 V' and the time axis '½T', 'T'
findings.what: The working row tells him the one thing the puzzle tests, that each tooth is a ramp, and the screen never says what T stands for; try 'One tooth: 0 V to 30 V in a time T'.

findings.where: Step 1 at 360 px light, opening frame
findings.what: For the first two seconds or so there is a blank band about 100 CSS px tall between the graph's time label and Play again, where the three working rows will arrive; show the first row at once, or show the rows faded, so the opening does not look half-built.

findings.where: SHOW steps 5 'Square, mean, root' and 7 'The fold'
findings.what: Each carries about 125 to 135 words and ten or so numbers under the drawing, which is heavy reading on a phone; trim each to the claim and the picture's why, and leave the rest of the working to the rows in the drawing.

findings.where: Contact sheets i10.a2.film-s0, s2, s4, s6 and s8
findings.what: At 3000 px wide the Read tool shows each sheet at about 300 px, so I could follow the order of the motion (area grows, then the rectangle rises; bars arrive and thin from 4 to 100; humps lift, slide and settle; the waves draw in turn, then the mean, RMS and form-factor rows) and saw nothing pop in, but I could not check labels by eye; the automated report finds nothing clipped or overflowing, and fewer, larger frames per sheet would let a reviewer check them.
